title: Hidden Global Operational Dependencies
pattern: Domain logic obtains mutable shared state or connections through global statics, static Singletons, or lazy-static definitions, or a struct constructor or builder silently resolves its configuration from a global context, instead of declaring the dependency as an argument or field.
why_bad: Hidden global dependencies couple code to a single operational instance, complicate isolated and parallel tests because shared state must be set up beforehand, and make initialization requirements and the replacement or mocking of configuration or infrastructure difficult to see; swapping the global requires modifying all calling code.
detection: Inspect global-static and singleton-registry accesses at two sites: (1) inside domain logic functions or private helper methods for operational state such as pools, connections, or mutable registries; (2) inside standard constructors or initialization methods for configuration lookup. Establish that the dependency is hidden from the function arguments, the object fields supplied at construction, or an explicit framework-managed injection contract.
counterexample: Truly immutable, global compile-time constants (such as physical constants or mathematical values) that bear zero operational volatility are not operational dependencies. Framework-level dependency injectors that explicitly annotate dependencies and manage construction lifetimes are not implicit constructor lookup merely because the framework maintains a registry, though manual constructor injection is still safer.
source: Erich Gamma et al., *Design Patterns* (1994), "Singleton"; Michael Feathers, *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* (2004), Chapter 9 ("The Case of the Irritating Global Dependency"), pp. 120-124; Michael Feathers, *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* (2004), Chapter 14 ("Dependencies on Globals"); Andrew Hunt & David Thomas, *The Pragmatic Programmer* (2019), Chapter 2 ("Globalization").
